title: Lean redesign of the silver diamine fluoride pathway in a 23-school dental programme
subtitle: Lean project with a measurement strand and a conversation strand, reported side by side
statement: In a school dental programme serving 23 primary schools, only 41 percent of children with an active cavity at screening received silver diamine fluoride at the next clinic visit last spring. Therapists attribute the gap to the flow of the clinic day: late or missing consent, a separate consent for SDF, children called from class in timetable order, and time spent explaining staining by phone. The project will redesign the pathway with lean methods and judge it by two separate kinds of evidence: timely treatment and chair time, and the views of parents, teachers and therapists, with attention to families who speak little English.
whoAffected: Children aged about 5 to 11 with active cavities, their parents, class teachers and school office staff, and four dental therapists.
whatHurts: Untreated cavities cause pain, infection and missed school; waiting for consent and searching for children wastes scarce clinic time; staining on front teeth can distress families.
currentPractice: Screening visit, separate consent forms sent home in school bags, SDF at a later clinic day if consent returns, children called in timetable order, staining explained by phone.
whyNow: SDF is newly available to therapists, uptake is low, and the school board is ready to consider a combined consent form.
constraints: No research grant; a data analyst one day a week. Changes must not add clinic days or therapist hours. Consent materials must be approved by the school board before use. Photographs of children's teeth may not leave the programme's clinical record system.
patientCenteredGoal: Every child with an active cavity is offered timely, acceptable treatment, and no family is left out because of language or a lost form.
summary: Problem framed as a lean redesign of a treatment pathway with two separately measured strands.
